subject: Computer Networking
title: How Enterprise Switches Work
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on How Enterprise Switches Work.

hook.text: A home switch has 8 ports. Enterprise switches have 48 and handle millions of packets per second.

buildup.text: Enterprise switches use ASICs — custom chips built solely for switching. They forward in hardware, not software.

discovery.text: They keep a MAC address table mapping each address to a port. Lookups happen in nanoseconds.

twist.text: Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops. Without it, a cable in two ports creates a broadcast storm.

climax.text: Stacking lets multiple switches act as one unit. 48 ports become 192 with one management interface.

punchline.text: Enterprise switches move data at wire speed. Zero waste.

quiz.question: Why do enterprise switches use ASICs?
options: To forward packets in hardware at maximum speed

details.summary: Enterprise switches support VLAN segmentation, spanning tree protocol, port security, Quality of Service, and stacking for high-availability deployments. They use ASIC-based forwarding to handle millions of packets per second with microsecond latency at scale.
details.whyItMatters: Enterprise switches provide the performance, security, and manageability that business networks require. They enable network segmentation and policy enforcement at wire speed.
takeaways: Enterprise switches use ASICs for wire-speed packet forwarding
VLANs segment traffic for security and performance isolation
Stacking combines multiple switches into one logical unit

faq.question: What makes an enterprise switch different from a home switch?
faq.answer: Enterprise switches add management features like VLANs, access control lists, SNMP monitoring, port mirroring, link aggregation, and spanning tree protocol. They offer higher port density, redundant power supplies, and are built for 24/7 operation in rack-mounted environments.

faq.question: What is switch stacking?
faq.answer: Stacking connects multiple physical switches through high-speed cables so they operate as a single logical switch. This simplifies management, provides redundancy if one switch fails, and allows link aggregation across multiple physical switches for higher bandwidth.
